title: Magic Eye Illusions
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore Magic Eye illusions and autostereograms, tracing the history from Ptolemy and early theories of binocular vision through Wheatstone's stereoscope, Brewster, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Bela Julesz's random dot stereogram, to Christopher Tyler's single-image autostereogram and its 1990s boom via Tom Baschet's Magic Eye company, Japanese publisher Tenyo, and Hallusion Art Prints. They cover the science of depth perception, how the posters are made, viewing tricks, and their use in treating stereo blindness and strabismus. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about Fahrenheit-to-Celsius conversion.
topics: how to see Magic Eye images

segments.title: Tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts announce fall tour stops in Orlando, Nashville, and Atlanta and point listeners to the tour page.

segments.title: Opening banter about Magic Eye
segments.summary: Hosts joke about seeing hidden images in Magic Eye posters and their experience with the technique, and Josh defines a magic eye poster or stereogram.

segments.title: Early theories of vision
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh introduce binocular vision and depth perception, then cover Ptolemy's extramission idea and the later theories of Ibn al-Haytham and Kepler and Descartes, which were partly wrong.

segments.title: Wheatstone and the stereoscope
segments.summary: Charles Wheatstone's 1830s stereoscope showed each eye flat, slightly different images, proving the brain fuses them into depth.

segments.title: Victorian stereoscope craze and stereographs
segments.summary: David Brewster made a handheld stereoscope, and the device became a popular parlor fad after the 1851 Great Exhibition. Oliver Wendell Holmes popularized the term stereograph and the viewers were used for scenic and risque images.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Brief transition into a break before the next segment.

segments.title: Bela Julesz and the random dot stereogram
segments.summary: Bela Julesz at Bell Labs created the random dot stereogram, showing that depth emerges from matching random dots in two images, without recognizable objects.

segments.title: Christopher Tyler and the single-image autostereogram
segments.summary: In the 1970s Christopher Tyler and programmer Maureen Clark created the autostereogram, a single image hiding depth in a repeating pattern.

segments.title: Tom Baschet, Pentica ad and Japanese launch
segments.summary: Tom Baschet at Pentica made a mime-based ad and an autostereogram ad, received requests for custom images, then started mail-order sales through Anything Enterprises and partnered with Tenyo in Japan, whose first book sold well.

segments.title: Magic Eye US boom and books
segments.summary: The first US Magic Eye book came out in 1993 and became a bestseller. Stereogram images appeared on cereal boxes, postcards, and corporate materials, and sales were estimated in the hundreds of millions in 1994.

segments.title: Hallusion Art Prints competition and mall kiosks
segments.summary: Hallusion Art Prints, founded by Paul Huber and Mike Belinsky, made higher-quality posters sold at mall kiosks, facing competition from cheaper versions.

segments.title: Fad decline and Magic Eye company history
segments.summary: Baschet sold his majority stake, and Cherry Smith renamed the company Magic Eye and still owns it. Stereograms remained useful for treating stereo blindness and strabismus.

segments.title: How Magic Eye images are made and how to view them
segments.summary: Hosts explain that auto-stereograms encode depth from grayscale, with lighter areas closer, and that viewers relax their eyes or unfocus. Chuck describes the nose-trick and two-dot methods.

segments.title: Listener mail on Celsius conversion
segments.summary: A listener named Jake Eichenberger corrects the hosts' Fahrenheit-to-Celsius math from a short stuff episode and shares his own mental method.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send email and the hosts sign off with the iHeartRadio credit.
